title: Invention of writing
summary: Writing, the recording of a language in visible signs, was invented independently at least four times: in southern Mesopotamia and Egypt around 3300–3100 BCE, in Shang China by about 1200 BCE, and in Mesoamerica during the first millennium BCE.
card: The oldest known writing comes from Uruk in southern Iraq, where temple administrators listed goods and labour on clay tablets around 3200 BCE, and from Tomb U-j at Abydos in Egypt, radiocarbon-dated to about 3320 BCE. Diviners at the Shang court in Anyang were using a mature Chinese script on bone and shell by about 1220 BCE, and Mesoamerican scripts appear by the middle of the first millennium BCE. Most scholars now count these as separate inventions, but which came first, and whether clay counting tokens gave rise to cuneiform, are still argued.
what:
Writing is a system of visible marks that records a particular language, as distinct from pictures, tallies or emblems that convey meaning without fixing words. The Oriental Institute's survey Visible Language (Woods, ed., 2010) identifies four 'pristine' inventions, made without any exposure to an existing script: in Mesopotamia, Egypt, China and Mesoamerica. Other scripts are thought likely to derive from, or to have been inspired by, these four.

In Mesopotamia the earliest tablets come from the Eanna temple precinct at Uruk, a city of perhaps 20,000–50,000 people covering about 2.5 km² in the Late Uruk period (c. 3350–3100 BCE). The German Archaeological Institute excavated about five thousand proto-cuneiform tablets there between 1928 and 1976, and the whole corpus now numbers roughly six thousand tablets and fragments. Because they were found discarded in rubbish fill, their dates are approximate: the earlier script phase, Uruk IV, is conventionally placed about 3200 BCE and the later Uruk III phase about 3100 BCE, while a single charcoal sample points to 3500–3390 BCE. Almost all are administrative records of goods, rations and labour.

In Egypt, Günter Dreyer's re-excavation of Tomb U-j in the royal cemetery of Umm el-Qa'ab at Abydos recovered nearly 200 incised bone and ivory tags and 125 ink inscriptions on pottery, dated by radiocarbon to about 3320 BCE. The signs mainly record names of places, institutions and rulers, and some already use the rebus principle.

In China, the earliest certain writing is the oracle-bone inscriptions from Anyang, records of royal divinations made under the last nine Shang kings (c. 1220–1050 BCE). In Mesoamerica, Olmec and Zapotec scripts preceded Maya writing; a carved monument at San José Mogote in Oaxaca is dated to about 600 BCE, and the earliest known Maya text, at San Bartolo in Guatemala, to 300–200 BCE. Early Mesoamerican scripts remain largely undeciphered.

Scholars still disagree about which invention came first, because the Abydos radiocarbon dates have been questioned and the Uruk tablets cannot be closely dated, and about whether Mesopotamian clay tokens were the direct ancestors of cuneiform signs.

uncertainty.note: Start: Tomb U-j at Abydos, c. 3320 BCE by calibrated radiocarbon (Boehmer, Dreyer and Kromer 1993, as cited in Visible Language), a dating others have questioned (Hendrickx 2006); Bayesian modelling puts the Naqada IID/IIIA transition, when Egyptian writing first appears, at 3377–3238 BCE (95%). Uruk IV is conventionally c. 3200 BCE; a lone charcoal sample from tablet contexts gives 3500–3390 BCE. End: the Mesoamerican invention is placed in the Early or Middle Formative (c. 1200–600 BCE); the earliest dated inscriptions are at San José Mogote (c. 600 BCE) and San Bartolo (300–200 BCE). China's earliest certain writing (c. 1220–1050 BCE) falls between these bounds.

how:
In Mesopotamia writing grew out of administration. Uruk's rapid growth in the later fourth millennium BCE created institutions that had to track rations, livestock, materials and labour. Before writing, accountants used small clay tokens, some sealed inside hollow clay envelopes whose outer surface could be impressed with the tokens inside, an interpretation first proposed by Pierre Amiet in the 1960s; then came numerical tablets carrying only number signs, and finally tablets that added one or two signs naming the commodity. Some proto-cuneiform numerals were made by pressing tokens into the clay, but most word signs were new pictographs, with a few borrowed from token shapes and from temple emblems such as Inana's symbol. Uruk IV signs were drawn with a pointed stylus; in the Uruk III phase about a century later their lines were straightened and impressed with a stylus of triangular cross-section, the beginning of wedge-shaped cuneiform. The system soon reached Jemdet Nasr, Khafajah and Tell Uqair, and possibly inspired proto-Elamite writing in Iran about 3100 BCE.

All four pristine systems started from logograms, signs for whole words, extended them with the rebus principle (using a sign for its sound to write a different word), and developed semantic determinatives. The Abydos tags already spell the town of Elephantine with an elephant over a hill sign. The settings differed: accounting at Uruk; labelling of goods and naming of elites, then royal display, in Egypt; divination on turtle shell and ox bone at the Shang court; and largely commemorative, calendrical texts in Mesoamerica. Some scholars argue that administrative records also existed in the latter cases on perishable papyrus, bamboo or bark. In every early state literacy was confined to a tiny elite, estimated at under 1 per cent of the population.
why_it_matters: Writing gave the first states a memory that outlasted any single official. Uruk's administrators could keep account of rations, labour and herds across years, and the technique spread across Babylonia within about a century and was later adapted to write unrelated languages, among them Akkadian, Elamite and Hittite. Over the following centuries writing moved beyond bookkeeping: in Mesopotamia letters, religious and historical texts appear only from the middle of the third millennium BCE, some seven hundred years after the first tablets. Writing also divides the human past into the documented and the undocumented, since from these points on rulers, places, prices and beliefs survive in their own terms, not only as objects in the ground. The Chinese script that descends from the Shang oracle-bone inscriptions is the only one of the four pristine systems still in use, so a continuous line of development runs from the Anyang diviners to Chinese writing today. The separate inventions matter as well: they show that writing was not a single lucky discovery that spread from Sumer, as scholars assumed in the mid-twentieth century, but something several societies arrived at for different reasons, from accounting to display, divination and commemoration. Without writing, early administrations would have depended on tokens, seals and the memory of officials, and knowledge of the ancient world would rest on archaeology alone. Because early literacy was confined to a small elite, the first written records also speak far more for temples and courts than for the farmers and workers they counted.

related.because: Farming economies brought the first clay counting tokens, which Schmandt-Besserat dates from about 7500 BCE, and ultimately the urban redistributive institutions at Uruk whose bookkeeping needs proto-cuneiform was invented to meet.

perspectives.holder: Ignace J. Gelb (A Study of Writing, 1952) and earlier proponents of monogenesis, as summarised by Woods (2010)
perspectives.account: Writing was invented only once, by the Sumerians; the idea, not the technology, then spread by 'stimulus diffusion' to Egypt and eventually China, while New World scripts were not true writing.

perspectives.holder: Christopher Woods and contributors to Visible Language (2010), reflecting current majority scholarship
perspectives.account: There were at least four independent, 'pristine' inventions (Mesopotamia, Egypt, China, Mesoamerica). Maya decipherment proved New World writing genuine, the Abydos finds made Egyptian writing as old as Mesopotamian, and the Chinese system is too different and too distant to derive from cuneiform.

perspectives.holder: Excavators of Tomb U-j (Dreyer and colleagues) and the Visible Language Egypt chapters; supported in broad terms by Dee et al. (2013)
perspectives.account: Egyptian writing at Abydos dates to about 3320 BCE by radiocarbon, at least as early as proto-cuneiform; Dee et al. find that Naqada IIIA, when writing first appears in Egypt, coincides closely with the first cuneiform.

perspectives.holder: Hendrickx (2006), as cited in Visible Language
perspectives.account: The calibrated radiocarbon dates for Tomb U-j are open to question, so Egyptian priority over Mesopotamia is not established; relative Naqada-period dating remains the preferred framework.

Egyptian writing can be modelled as a local development rooted in emblematic display, against the long-controversial hypothesis of Mesopotamian influence; its near-simultaneous emergence with cuneiform reflects related political and economic changes across the late fourth-millennium Near East.

Cuneiform evolved directly from a token accounting system: plain tokens from about 7500 BCE became numerals, complex tokens of the fourth millennium became word signs, and impressed envelopes (c. 3300 BCE) were the bridge to tablets.

perspectives.holder: Critics including Paul Zimansky (1993) and Christopher Woods (2010)
perspectives.account: Only the numeral signs clearly relate to token impressions; many proposed token-to-sign matches are implausible, and the token record is too scattered across millennia to be one uniform system.

perspectives.holder: Saturno, Stuart and Beltrán (2006), as reported by Mesoweb
perspectives.account: San Bartolo shows the Maya were writing by 300–200 BCE, nearly as early as any Mesoamerican script, and Maya writing may have influenced the Isthmian script rather than the reverse; Palka (2010) instead sees Maya writing as adopted from Olmec or Zapotec neighbours.
